chunks: "I'd start from what the board has to do and work upward from two layers, adding only when I can name the reason. First is routing density.
Look at the densest part: a fine pitch BGA, a QFN with lots of pins, or a big connector. If I can't escape the signals on top and bottom, I need more signal layers.
Anything with edges faster than a nanosecond or two, like USB, Ethernet, SDRAM or a fast SPI, wants a solid ground plane right below it so the return current path is short.
That alone pushes me to four layers: signal, ground, power, signal.
Third is power: a few rails and some high current points are much easier with a power plane or at least a second copper layer.
And fourth is EMI: a ground plane cuts loop area and the radiation that comes with it. Cost comes in last, but it's real.
Four layers cost noticeably more than two, six more than four, and HDI is another jump.
Sometimes a four-layer board is actually cheaper overall because it is much smaller or needs fewer respins.
I'd sketch the stackup early, route the hardest block first, and bump the layer count only when something genuinely won't route or won't pass."
